steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The problem of evil and suffering challenges the idea of an omnipotent, loving God. If God is all-powerful and all-loving, why does suffering exist? This is a key philosophical debate in GCSE RS.

steps.title: Exam Tip
steps.body: The word "Trinity" comes from "tri" meaning three and "unity" meaning one. The doctrine was formally established at the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE. The Trinity is not explicitly mentioned in the Bible but is inferred from passages like Matthew 28:19.

steps.title: RS Exam Tips — The Nature of God
steps.body: 1. For The Nature of God questions, always include specific scriptural or source references where relevant 2. Explain both religious and non-religious viewpoints 3. Use specialist vocabulary precisely (e.g. terms from the specification) 4. Evaluate by analysing strengths and weaknesses of different views before reaching your conclusion 5. Link your discussion of The Nature of God to its real-world impact on believers and society

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Explain two Christian beliefs about the nature of God. | Q: How does the problem of evil challenge Christian beliefs about God?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: 1) God is omnipotent — Christians believe God is all-powerful and nothing is beyond God's ability, as shown in Genesis where God creates the universe from nothing. 2) God is loving — Christians believ | The problem of evil challenges the idea that God is both omnipotent and loving. If God is all-powerful, God could prevent suffering; if God is all-loving, God would want to. The existence of suffering

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always refer to specific sources of authority (scripture, sacred texts, religious leaders) Explain contrasting beliefs — different views within and between traditions Use key terminology precisely (e.g. tawhid, atonement, sanctity of life) For 12-mark evaluation questions, consider both sides before reaching a justified conclusion Link beliefs to their impact on individuals, communities and society Acknowledge diversity — no religious tradition has a single, uniform view
